title: Cashmere vs Merino Wool: Which Is Warmer, Softer, and Worth the Price?
excerpt: Cashmere and merino are the two most-loved luxury fibers. We compare warmth, softness, price, and care so you can pick the right one for your wardrobe.
content:
Choosing between cashmere and merino wool is one of the most common questions in knitwear. Both are premium natural fibers, but they behave very differently on the body and in the laundry basket.

The clearest difference is fiber fineness. High-grade cashmere measures roughly 14.5 to 19 microns, while merino wool typically ranges from 17 to 24 microns, with the finest superfine merino dropping below 18.5 microns. Because cashmere is finer and its fibers are shorter and softer, it feels lighter and silkier against the skin, making it the better close-to-skin layer for many people who find wool itchy.

When it comes to warmth, merino is actually the harder worker per gram. Merino fibers are crimped and elastic, trapping more air and regulating temperature in a wider range of conditions, which is why merino dominates base layers and performance wear. Cashmere, by contrast, offers soft, drapey warmth that is more refined and less athletic. A cashmere sweater keeps you warm with less bulk, but it is not built for high-output activity the way merino is.

Price is where the two diverge sharply. Cashmere comes from the fine undercoat of cashmere goats, and each goat produces only a small amount of usable fiber each year, which pushes prices up. Merino is harvested from sheep in much larger volumes, so it is more affordable at comparable levels of quality.

For most wardrobes, the smart move is to keep both. Reach for merino when you need performance, travel versatility, or a sturdier sweater that can take friction. Save cashmere for the pieces that should feel luxurious, calm, and soft against the skin.

title: How to Wash Cashmere Without Ruining It: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: Cashmere needs a gentle hand-wash routine, not the machine's regular cycle. Here is the exact method to keep sweaters soft, shaped, and fuzz-free.
content:
Washing cashmere is not difficult, but it does require a gentler routine than most people expect. The good news is that cashmere does not need washing often, a few times a season is usually plenty.

Start by turning the sweater inside out and spot-treating any marks with a little mild wool detergent. Fill a basin with cool or lukewarm water, never hot, and dissolve a capful of pH-neutral wool or cashmere shampoo into it. Submerge the garment, press it gently, and let it soak for 15 to 20 minutes. Avoid scrubbing, wringing, or twisting, which distorts the fibers and causes pilling.

Rinse with clean cool water until the water runs clear, then press the water out with your palms rather than squeezing. Roll the sweater in a clean dry towel to absorb most of the moisture, then lay it flat on a drying rack or a fresh towel, reshaping the collar, cuffs, and seams while it is still damp. Never hang cashmere to dry, the weight of the wet knit stretches the shoulders and neckline permanently.

If you prefer the washing machine, use the wool or hand-wash cycle with cold water, a wool-specific detergent, and place the garment in a mesh laundry bag. Remove it promptly and dry flat.

A final tip: wash cashmere alone or with other cashmere, avoid fabric softener, which coats the fibers and dulls their softness, and refresh between washes by airing the sweater out overnight. Follow this routine and your knits will keep their shape, softness, and colour for years.

title: Cashmere Grades Explained: What A, B, and C Really Mean
excerpt: Not all cashmere is created equal. We explain the A, B, and C grading system, what fiber diameter and length tell you, and how to spot quality.
content:
When a sweater is labelled simply "cashmere," it hides a wide range of quality. The industry grades cashmere primarily by fiber diameter, measured in microns, and by fiber length, both of which shape how soft, durable, and expensive the finished knit will be.

In simple terms, grade A cashmere is the finest and longest. Its fibers typically fall below 15.5 to 16 microns with good staple length, producing the softest, most resilient hand feel and the least pilling. This is the grade used by premium brands for garments that should last and feel luxurious next to the skin.

Grade B cashmere is slightly thicker, often around 17 to 18.5 microns, and may contain shorter or slightly coarser fibers. It is still genuinely soft and comfortable, but the surface is a little less refined and it may show wear a touch sooner. Many mid-range garments fall here.

Grade C cashmere is the coarsest and shortest, often above 18.5 microns. It feels noticeably more like wool, pills more readily, and is the least durable. It is still cashmere under the fibre-content label, but it delivers far less of the softness people expect.

The honest takeaway is that micron count is the single most useful number a buyer can ask for. A label that states "cashmere" tells you the fibre, but the grade tells you the quality. At JINHEXI we specify the fiber fineness and grade we work with because softer, longer fibers are exactly what make a sweater worth keeping season after season.

title: Why Mongolian Cashmere Is Prized: Fiber, Grade, and Supply
excerpt: Mongolian cashmere is famous for its fineness. We look at where it comes from, how it is harvested, and why the region dominates premium knitwear.
content:
Mongolia, along with China's Inner Mongolia region, supplies the vast majority of the world's cashmere. The reason is geography and breeding: cashmere goats there evolved to grow a fine, dense undercoat to survive extreme continental winters, and that undercoat is the cashmere itself.

Harvesting is a careful, seasonal process. In spring, when the goats naturally begin shedding, herders comb out the soft undercoat by hand rather than shearing it off. Each goat yields only a small amount of usable cashmere each year, typically a few hundred grams before cleaning removes coarse guard hairs, dirt, and grease. By the time it reaches the mill, only a fraction of the original combed fiber remains.

What makes Mongolian cashmere distinctive is fineness. Because of the cold climate and breeding stock, much of the region's cashmere falls into the finer grades, often below 16 to 17 microns, which translates directly into softer, lighter, more drapey knitwear.

Supply is the bigger story for buyers. Because production is seasonal and concentrated, cashmere prices can swing noticeably from year to year with weather, herder numbers, and global demand. That is why responsible brands build relationships with suppliers, buy with a longer view, and avoid chasing the cheapest fiber on the market.

At JINHEXI we source 100% cashmere with an emphasis on fine, long-staple fiber, because the region and the grade are what allow a sweater to be both soft now and durable for years.

title: Why Does Cashmere Cost So Much? What You're Really Paying For
excerpt: A cashmere sweater can cost ten times more than wool. We break down the real economics: fiber yield, hand harvesting, processing loss, and grading.
content:
The price gap between a cashmere sweater and a wool sweater looks shocking until you understand what sits behind it. Cashmere is expensive for concrete, physical reasons that start at the farm.

The first factor is yield. Cashmere comes from the fine undercoat of cashmere goats, and each goat produces only a small amount of usable fiber per year, far less than a single sheep produces in wool. On top of that, the raw combed fiber loses a large share of its weight during cleaning and dehairing, when coarse guard hairs and impurities are removed. What reaches the mill is a fraction of what left the herder.

Second is labor. The fiber is combed out by hand in a seasonal window, sorted, dehaired, graded, spun, and knitted. Every one of these steps is skilled and slow compared with commodity wool processing. The finer the grade, the more careful the handling and the more it costs.

Third is grading and wastage. Only the finest, longest fibers command the premium prices. Thicker, shorter fibers become cheaper garments, so a truly soft, durable sweater requires the better material, and that material is genuinely scarce.

Finally, there is simple supply and demand. Cashmere production is concentrated and seasonal, prices fluctuate with global demand, and the finest fiber is limited. When a brand prices a cashmere piece honestly, you are paying for fiber fineness, hand skill, processing, and a material that is naturally rare.

At JINHEXI we aim to price cashmere fairly, not cheaply, because the fiber, the grade, and the construction are what make the sweater worth wearing year after year.

title: Sweater Yarn Weight Explained: Count, Ply, and Gauge for Winter Knits
excerpt: Yarn count, ply, and gauge decide how warm and how fine a sweater feels. A plain-English guide to the numbers on a knitwear label.
content:
The numbers and terms on a knitwear label can feel like a code. Yarn count, ply, and gauge all describe the yarn behind the garment, and they directly control warmth, weight, drape, and durability.

Yarn count refers to the fineness of the spun yarn. A higher count means a finer, thinner yarn, which knits into a lighter, softer, more delicate fabric. Lower-count yarns are thicker and heavier, producing sturdier, more structured sweaters. Finer yarn is generally more expensive to spin and requires more skill, which is why high-count cashmere commands a premium.

Ply describes how many strands are twisted together to make the final yarn. A single-ply yarn is fine and soft but less durable, while a two-ply or three-ply yarn is stronger, holds its shape better, and is usually the right choice for everyday sweaters that need to last. The ply count is a good quick signal of durability.

Gauge (or knit gauge) refers to how many stitches fit across a fixed width, which reflects the density of the knit. A finer gauge creates a smoother, more refined surface with finer detail, ideal for elegant, close-fitting knits. A coarser gauge produces a chunkier, more relaxed, more casual texture.

When you combine the three, a high-count, multi-ply, fine-gauge cashmere yarn gives you a soft, durable, refined sweater that drapes beautifully, which is exactly the combination premium knitwear is built on.

Understanding these terms helps you read between the lines on a label and choose a sweater for how you will actually wear it, close to the skin, layered, or as a statement piece.

title: How to Style a Cashmere Sweater for Work: 7 Effortless Looks
excerpt: A cashmere sweater is the easiest route to an elevated work wardrobe. Seven outfit formulas that take it from meeting room to evening without fuss.
content:
A good cashmere sweater is the workhorse of a professional wardrobe because it is polished on its own and layers effortlessly. These seven looks cover everything from a boardroom day to a more relaxed office.

1. Cashmere crewneck with tailored trousers. The most foolproof formula: a fine-gauge crewneck in a neutral tone with high-waisted tailored trousers and a simple leather shoe. Clean, modern, and appropriate for almost any meeting.

2. Cashmere turtleneck under a blazer. A slim turtleneck adds warmth and polish under a structured blazer. Keep the palette tonal, navy, charcoal, or camel, and let the knit do the work.

3. Cashmere cardigan as a top layer. A longer cardigan worn open over a blouse or a fine tee reads as a soft alternative to a jacket, especially in creative or relaxed workplaces.

4. Cashmere sweater with a midi skirt. For a softer silhouette, pair a close-fitting cashmere top with a flowing midi skirt and heeled boots. The contrast of knit and drape looks considered, not fussy.

5. Layered cashmere on a cold commute. A thin cashmere layer under a wool coat adds serious warmth without bulk, so you stay elegant even in low temperatures.

6. Monochrome cashmere. Wearing the same tone head to toe, sweater, trousers, and outerwear, looks expensive and effortless. Choose one neutral and vary the textures.

7. Cashmere with denim for casual Friday. A quality cashmere sweater instantly upgrades dark denim, giving a relaxed but intentional finish that works for hybrid offices.

Whatever the look, the key is a well-fitting, high-grade sweater in a versatile neutral. That one piece quietly lifts everything around it.

title: How to Store Cashmere and Keep Moths Away for Good
excerpt: Moths love cashmere. Here is how to fold, store, and protect your knits so they come out of the cupboard clean, fresh, and hole-free.
content:
Cashmere is a natural protein fiber, which makes it a favourite food source for clothes moths. A few simple habits will keep your sweaters safe through the off-season.

The first rule is to wash before storing. Moths and their larvae are attracted to sweat, skin cells, and food stains, so never put a worn sweater away unwashed. Follow a gentle wash routine and make sure the garment is completely dry before storage.

Second, fold, never hang. Hanging stretches the shoulders and neckline under the garment's own weight. Fold sweaters neatly and stack them in a way that distributes the weight, or roll them to save space.

Third, choose the right container. Airtight storage boxes or sealed garment bags create a barrier that moths cannot easily reach. If you use a wardrobe, store cashmere on a shelf in a sealed bag rather than open to the air.

Fourth, add natural deterrents. Cedar blocks, lavender sachets, and moth-repellent strips placed in the container discourage moths without the harsh smell of naphthalene. Refresh the cedar or lavender periodically as their scent fades.

Finally, inspect regularly. Check stored knits every few weeks for the first signs of moth activity, small holes, silk webbing, or cast skins. Catching an infestation early is far easier than repairing a damaged sweater.

With clean, folded, sealed storage and a little natural protection, your cashmere will stay soft, fresh, and hole-free until winter comes around again.

title: Sustainable Cashmere: What 'Responsible' Really Means in 2026
excerpt: Not every 'sustainable' claim is equal. We break down traceability, animal welfare, land impact, and what to look for in responsibly sourced cashmere.
content:
As consumers ask more about the origins of their clothing, "sustainable cashmere" has become a common label. But the term covers a lot, and not every claim carries the same weight.

Traceability is the foundation. Responsible cashmere can be traced from the herder or cooperative back to the finished garment. This matters because overgrazing and land degradation are real concerns in cashmere regions, and traceability helps buyers verify that fiber is not contributing to pasture damage. Look for brands and suppliers that can name their source regions and supply chain.

Animal welfare is the second pillar. Cashmere is combed from live goats during the natural spring shed, which is far gentler than shearing and less invasive when done well. Responsible sourcing verifies that herders treat animals humanely and that the income supports the communities who produce the fiber.

Third is fiber efficiency and durability. The most sustainable garment is the one that lasts. High-grade, long-staple cashmere pills less and survives more seasons, which reduces the need to replace it. Buying better and wearing longer is itself a sustainability choice.

Finally, look for verified programs. Certifications and audited supply chains, such as those tied to the cashmere life cycle assessments and responsible sourcing standards, provide more reliable signals than vague marketing. In 2026, brands are increasingly publishing sourcing data rather than just claims.

At JINHEXI, responsible sourcing means asking our partners about region, fiber grade, and animal welfare, and being transparent about what we can and cannot verify. A softer, longer-lasting sweater made with care is the most honest version of sustainability we can offer.

title: Cashmere 101: A Beginner's Guide to Buying Your First Sweater
excerpt: Buying your first cashmere sweater can feel risky. Here is what to check on the label, in your hands, and in the price before you commit.
content:
A first cashmere sweater is a real investment, so it pays to know what you are looking at. These checks will help you choose a piece that stays soft and keeps its shape for years.

Start with the fiber content label. Look for 100% cashmere, and be cautious of blends that use only a small percentage of cashmere to justify a higher price. The label should state the fiber clearly and honestly.

Next, feel the fabric. Quality cashmere feels soft and smooth against the skin with a gentle, clean hand feel. If it feels coarse, wiry, or itchy, the fiber is likely a lower grade. Rub the surface gently to gauge how much fuzz it produces; finer, longer fiber fuzzes far less.

Check the construction. Look at the seams, ribbing, and collar. Neat, even stitching, secure seams, and a properly shaped neckline signal careful production. A multi-ply yarn, such as two-ply or three-ply, is more durable than a fine single ply.

Consider the weight and gauge. A finer, high-count knit feels lighter and more refined, while a chunkier gauge is more casual. Choose based on how you will wear it, close to the skin, layered, or as a statement piece.

Then think about price honestly. Genuine high-grade cashmere cannot be extremely cheap because the fiber itself is scarce and costly. A very low price usually means thinner fiber, a lower grade, or a heavy synthetic blend. You do not need the most expensive option, but expect to pay a fair price for real quality.

Finally, choose a versatile colour and a classic silhouette you will actually wear. A well-chosen first sweater in a neutral tone will earn its place in your wardrobe for many winters to come.

title: Why Knitwear Pills and How to Slow It Down
excerpt: Woolmark describes pilling as surface abrasion, which is why sleeves and elbows show it first.
content: Pilling is usually a sign of friction, not a sign that the garment failed. Woolmark explains that abrasion during wear creates the fuzzy surface balls people notice on sleeves, elbows, and side seams first. The practical fix is straightforward: reduce rubbing, avoid fabric softener, wash gently, and use a de-pilling tool if a sweater starts to fuzz.
